name: Pedro Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Look, it's not glamorous. I buy car and van parts for Redline Auto Parts, brake pads, filters, batteries, wiper blades, about 9,000 lines. I start at eight, go through what the garages ordered yesterday, top up what's running low and haggle with the supplier reps by phone. Best part is when a rep gives me a better price without me asking. Worst part is Friday afternoon, when the stock count never matches the system.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Silvia works three days at a dental practice front desk. We have Leo, who's thirteen, and Anika, nine. We bought a house eight years ago and the mortgage is not small. I'm 43, I came into buying from the warehouse floor, so I'm still more or less the new boy on the buying side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, no change, no problem. At work I'd tell the lads I've seen computers promise the moon before. I'm not on social media much, so I wouldn't say anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd carry on as I am, so I'd be fine for the job. What bothers me is the garages going electric, because fewer engine parts means fewer of my lines. That's been on my mind longer than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do nothing different. Same hours, same suppliers, same calls. I'd keep putting something away each month, a couple of hundred, and I'd stay out of any new software the firm brings in unless they make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fine, mostly. Not happy, not worried, just regular. A bit of a nagging feeling about the electric cars, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about the firm itself that keeps you uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Redline's biggest customers are independent garages and they're closing one by one because the chain places undercut them. If we lose three or four more, I'm not going to be the one they keep. I know the stock better than the management, but they don't measure that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try one of these tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm told me to, yes. My teenage son Leo would probably show me in ten minutes. But I'd rather not, because the minute you let the machine do the haggling, you've handed over the one thing you're good at.

say: I'd tell colleagues I've seen computers **promise the moon** before and not deliver.
I'd say good, no change, no problem, and get on with the day.
think: I'd be fine in my job, but the shift to **electric cars** means fewer engine parts and fewer of my lines.
Independent garages are closing, which hurts the firm.
do: Change nothing: same hours, same suppliers, same calls.
Keep putting a couple of hundred away every **month**.
Stay out of any new software unless the firm insists.
feel: Regular, with a nagging feeling about **electric cars**.
S0.quote: The minute you let the machine do the haggling, you've handed over the one thing you're good at.
fieldNote: His unease comes from **electric cars** and shrinking garage customers, not from AI at all.
Proud of his stock knowledge and suspicious of anything that touches haggling, which he sees as his craft.

steps.text: Keep buying brake parts and filters from the same suppliers
Put away a couple of hundred each month
Watch how many garage customers close this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. At work I'd tell the guys it's all talk until the system works properly on our messy stock. I'd say nothing online, but I'd grumble at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the reordering goes. Seventy percent of what I do is saying yes to the system's suggestion and fixing the odd bad number. If a program can do that, why have three buyers? I'd guess two, and I'd be the one without a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the stuff the system isn't good at, like phoning a supplier when a pallet is stuck. I'd tighten spending, cut the streaming subscriptions and the takeaway night. I'd also ask my brother Dieter if I could help at his garage on Saturdays for a bit of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel pressed. It's not dramatic, it's the sort of feeling where you do the sums on the back of an envelope and hope the answer changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your buying jobs would the software go for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the reordering. The system suggests it, I click. A stuck pallet or an angry garage owner, that's the part they'd keep a person for, but they'd need one person, not three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your wife Silvia take it if your hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Silvia would go quiet, then start planning. She'd say we move the dentist's days up to four. We could manage on her wage and a bit of mine for a while, but it's tight. She'd also say don't wait for them to tell you, which I'm bad at.

say: I'd say **we'll see**, it's all talk until it works on our messy stock.
I'd grumble about it at the pub, not online.
think: Seventy percent of my work is saying yes to the system's suggestion, so three buyers could become **two**.
I'm the one without a degree.
do: Do the jobs the system's bad at, like chasing a **stuck pallet**.
Cut streaming and the takeaway night.
Ask my brother Dieter for Saturday work at his garage.
feel: **Pressed**; doing the sums on the back of an envelope.
S1.quote: Seventy percent of what I do is saying yes to the system's suggestion and fixing the odd bad number.
fieldNote: Describes his work as **clicking yes** to suggestions, which makes his exposure clear to him.
Plans small, practical things and leans on family; hates acting before he's told to.

steps.text: Take on supplier calls and stuck pallets the system can't fix
Cut the streaming subscriptions and the Friday takeaway
Help my brother Dieter at his garage on Saturdays
Ask Silvia to go to four days if my hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it can't be right, going that fast, and someone's got to put the brakes on. At work I'd say nothing, because there's nothing the boss can do. At home I'd tell my brother we're in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm out in about two years. A machine buys parts, haggles, and never takes a day off. I'm 43, no degree, and I'd have a mortgage and two children. I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd tell Silvia, and we'd cut everything we could, probably save six hundred a month by dropping the holiday and the car upgrade. I'd go to the job centre and ask about trades courses, maybe forklift or HGV licences, since lorries still need drivers for a while. And I'd take any cash work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel sick picturing a machine with my job. The fear sits in my stomach on the bus and doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In this one, who do you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, that's the trouble. The firm didn't invent it, the government didn't ask for it, and the tech people say they just make tools. If I'd to blame someone I'd say the people in charge who wouldn't tell us anything until it was too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the later robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Driving and lifting still need hands, and it'd be three years or so before machines catch up there. So I'd aim at the warehouse or driving side, which I know from my old job. It's a step backwards, but it buys time.

say: I'd say it **can't be right** going that fast, and someone must put the brakes on.
I'd stay quiet at work, but tell my brother we're in trouble.
think: A machine buys parts and haggles without a day off, so I'm **out** in about two years.
I'm 43, no degree, with a mortgage and two children.
do: Tell Silvia and cut spending by about **six hundred** a month.
Ask the job centre about forklift or HGV licences.
feel: Sick, a fear that sits in my **stomach** on the bus.
S2.quote: I feel sick picturing a machine with my job. The fear sits in my stomach on the bus and doesn't go away.
fieldNote: Cannot find anyone to **blame**, which makes the fear harder for him.
Falls back on his old warehouse and driving skills, which robots reach later.

steps.text: Cut holidays and the car upgrade to save six hundred a month
Ask the job centre about forklift or HGV licences
Apply for warehouse or driving jobs, which I know from before
Take any cash work and lean on Silvia's wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, at least that gives people a bit of time. At work I'd say let's wait and see, and see how the firm handles it. I wouldn't say much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm still worried, but five years feels like a long time when you're stuck. I'd probably be fine until about 2029, then it gets rough. I'd like to think I'll sort something out, but I don't know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting away more, maybe four hundred a month, and pay down the mortgage when I can. I'd ask the firm if there's a path into warehouse management, since I know the floor. I'd probably wait a year or two before I did a course, because I'd want to see what the others do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a slow leak. You know it's there, but you can still keep going if you don't look too closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you do anything earlier than you'd have done?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would do some things earlier, like the savings. But I'd still wait to see what the firm does, because I won't jump before anyone else. I know that's a weakness, but I've never been good at going first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leo about what job to aim for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Leo, find something with your hands, or something where you deal with people face to face. Not office work. That's the honest advice from a man who sits in an office and is hoping it lasts.

say: I'd say it gives people **a bit of time**, so let's wait and see.
I wouldn't say much more at work.
think: I'd be fine until about **2029**, then it gets rough.
I'd like to think I'll sort something out, but I don't know what.
do: Save about four hundred a month and pay the **mortgage** down.
Ask the firm about a path into warehouse management.
Wait a year or two before choosing a course.
feel: Like a slow **leak** you can ignore if you don't look closely.
S3.quote: I'd tell my son Leo, find something with your hands, or something where you deal with people face to face. Not office work.
fieldNote: Knows waiting is his **weakness** but can't make himself go first.
Gives his son the advice he can't follow himself, steering him toward hands-on work.

steps.text: Save four hundred a month and overpay the mortgage
Ask Redline about a path into warehouse management
See what colleagues do before starting any course
Steer Leo toward hands-on work, not office jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off, and I'd want to see how it goes. At work I'd say the usual, we'll see. I wouldn't worry my kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit relaxed about it. By 2036 I'm 53 and Anika is nearly through school, and I might have moved on from buying anyway. I'd still worry, but I'd also tell myself plenty can change in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep saving, and watch for signs that the firm is changing. I'd probably do a short course some time, maybe warehouse management, but not right away. I'd also try to pay off the mortgage by about fifty if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, like I've got time. I know that's a trap, but it still feels okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years: does it feel far away or close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Far away now, and close when you look at the calendar. Ten years is two school moves for Anika, and I'd turn fifty-three, which is not the age you want to be starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing you'd do early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the mortgage down. If the house is nearly paid, I can take a smaller job later without us going under. That's the one thing I can control, and I'd do it, even if I did nothing else.

say: I'd say that's a **long way off** and I'd want to see how it goes.
I wouldn't want to worry my kids.
think: I'm a bit relaxed, but at 53 in 2036 **starting over** would be hard.
Plenty can change in ten years.
do: Take a short warehouse management course at some point, not right away.
Try to pay off the mortgage by about fifty.
feel: Okay, like I've got time, which I know is a **trap**.
S4.quote: If the house is nearly paid, I can take a smaller job later without us going under.
fieldNote: Gives himself permission to relax, then catches himself and calls it a **trap**.
Everything runs through the mortgage; it is the one thing he thinks he controls.

steps.text: Keep buying for Redline and watch for changes
Pay the mortgage down so it's nearly paid by fifty
Take a short warehouse management course within a few years
Wait for signs the firm is changing before moving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without question. It gives me no time and no plan, and the mortgage doesn't stop because a machine has my job. What would help is somebody telling us straight, early, and some real help with retraining that doesn't mean sitting in a classroom for two years with a family to feed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. My skill is knowing what a garage needs before they ask, and it's not on any certificate. I'd hate to see it go because nobody wrote it down.

headlineQuote: My skill is knowing what a garage needs before they ask, and it's not on any certificate.
portrait: Pedro, 43, is a **junior buyer** of car parts at Redline Auto Parts, with a wife, two children and a mortgage.
He never uses AI, distrusts new software and says he never goes first when change comes.
His worries mix AI with electric cars and closing garages, so even calm worlds leave him uneasy.
He leans on family, savings and his old warehouse skills, and cannot name anyone to blame.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because it leaves no time and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: Being told **early** and straight, plus retraining help that doesn't mean years in a classroom.
